body.en:
• A form wraps controls: <form method="post" action="register.php"> ... inputs ... <input type="submit"> </form>. Omit action and the form posts back to its own page.
  • The control kit: text box (name, city), password (masked), text area (feedback), radio (one-of-many, same name), checkbox (many-of-many; use name="hobby[]" to receive an array), select/option (dropdown), HTML5 types date, color, email, number, file, and buttons.
  • The name attribute is everything: it becomes the key in $_GET/$_POST. A control without a name submits nothing.
  • Group radios by shared name; give every option a distinct value - the browser sends the value, not the label.

• GET packs data into the URL query string (?city=Surat&seats=2): visible, bookmarkable, limited (~2 KB), and retried freely on refresh. Use for searches and filters.
  • POST sends data in the request body: invisible in the URL, effectively unlimited, required for uploads. Use for anything that changes state (register, book, pay).
  • Never put passwords or personal data in a GET URL - they land in browser history and server logs.
  • Refreshing a POST page re-submits (the classic double-booking hazard) - solved with the Post/Redirect/Get pattern in real apps.

• $_GET and $_POST are associative arrays of the incoming parameters; $_REQUEST merges both (plus cookies - prefer the specific one).
  • $_FILES carries upload records: name, type, size, tmp_name, error per file field.
  • $_SERVER describes the request: REQUEST_METHOD, SCRIPT_NAME, REMOTE_ADDR, headers. $_ENV holds environment variables; $GLOBALS every script-global variable.
  • All superglobals are available in every scope - no global declaration needed inside functions.
  • $_SESSION and $_COOKIE complete the family in Unit 4.

• One .php page both shows and handles a form: if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'POST') { validate + process } else { show form }.
  • Advantages: errors are shown beside the same form; entered values are re-echoed (sticky form) so users fix one field, not ten.
  • Sticky values: value="<?php echo htmlspecialchars($name ?? ''); ?>" - echo what the user typed, escaped.
  • Collect messages in an $errors array; show the list above the form when not empty.

• Presence: isset($_POST['name']) (exists, may be null-safe), empty($v) (missing or blank). Start every field with these two.
  • Shape: is_numeric(), strlen($s) >= 3, ctype_alpha(); filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL) returns the value or false; filter_var($n, FILTER_VALIDATE_INT) likewise for integers.
  • Clean before checking: trim() strips edge spaces; stripslashes() removes stray escapes; cast numbers with (int).
  • Rules live server-side only: HTML required/maxlength hints are trivially bypassed - the server is the bouncer, not the browser.
  • After validating, remember output safety separately: htmlspecialchars() on every echo of user data.

• Put it together: self-processing page + sticky values + $errors list + per-field rules.
  • Typical rules: name required, letters-minimum-3; email filter_var(..., FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL); mobile exactly 10 digits; age numeric 15-100; route from an allowed list; terms checkbox must be set.
  • Only when count($errors) === 0 do you accept: show the confirmation/summary, then (Units 4-5) remember the user or save to MySQL.
  • Sanity sample: our program posts email=not-an-email, age=abc - watch the validator catch both while echoing the rest back.

• Create and remove: mkdir("uploads"), rmdir("uploads") (only when empty); probe with is_dir()/file_exists().
  • List contents: scandir($dir) returns everything (includes . and .. - skip them); glob("uploads/*.png") filters by pattern.
  • Inspect files: is_file(), filesize(), filemtime() (last modified), basename()/pathinfo() split names and extensions.
  • Housekeeping mantra: check is_dir() before mkdir(), and never trust a filename from a browser - rebuild it yourself.

• Explicit trio: $h = fopen("feedback.txt", "a") → fwrite($h, $line) / fgets($h) → fclose($h). Modes: r read, w write-and-truncate, a append, + variants add the other direction.
  • Shortcuts: file_get_contents() reads whole; file_put_contents($f, $t, FILE_APPEND) appends in one call; file() returns an array of lines; fputcsv() writes CSV rows safely.
  • The feedback practical carries the full cycle: POST form → validate → append one CSV line → display all stored feedback.
  • Always check fopen's return (false = permission/path problem) before writing.

• The form needs method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data"; without the enctype, no file travels.
  • Server side: $_FILES['avatar'] holds name, type, size, tmp_name, error. If error === UPLOAD_ERR_OK, the file waits in a temp folder - move_uploaded_file($tmp, "uploads/".$safe) or it vanishes.
  • Verify: check the extension whitelist and size limit, confirm with getimagesize() that an image really is one, and basename() the name to strip path tricks.
  • Thumbnail cheat without GD: store once, display with a fixed <img width="64"> - the browser scales it.
  • Download: reply with headers - Content-Type: application/octet-stream and Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="..." - then readfile() the contents.

h.en: Sending Email: Plain, HTML and Attachments (Practical 15)

body.en:
• mail($to, $subject, $message, $headers) - headers carry From, Cc, Reply-To, and the MIME content type.
  • Plain text: default body - just send. HTML email: add Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 and compose the body with tags.
  • Attachments need MIME multipart: a boundary string, the message part, then the file base64-encoded - real projects use PHPMailer instead of hand-rolled MIME.
  • On XAMPP localhost, mail() returns false until an SMTP account is configured (sendmail.ini / Mercury) - so our program composes and displays the exact messages first, then reports the send attempt honestly.
  • Newsletter flow: validate email → store subscriber → send confirmation (plain + HTML versions).

$cases = [
    ["isset",     isset($_POST["ghost"]) ? "true" : "false (ghost never submitted)"],

title.en: File modes cookbook: r / w / a / w+

code.en:
<?php
$f = __DIR__ . "/log.txt";

// "w" - fresh write (truncates anything old)
$h = fopen($f, "w"); fwrite($h, "day 1: server up\n"); fclose($h);

// "a" - append keeps history
$h = fopen($f, "a"); fwrite($h, "day 2: added route BRC\n"); fclose($h);

// "r" - read line by line
echo "== read with fgets ==\n";
$h = fopen($f, "r");
while (!feof($h)) {
    $line = fgets($h);
    if ($line === false) break;
    echo "  " . rtrim($line) . "\n";
}
fclose($h);

// shortcuts
file_put_contents($f, "day 3: backup done\n", FILE_APPEND);
echo "== read whole at once ==\n";
echo file_get_contents($f);

// "w+" truncates then allows reading too
$h = fopen($f, "w+");
fwrite($h, "fresh start\n");
rewind($h);
echo "== w+ after truncate ==\n  " . rtrim(fgets($h)) . "\n";
fclose($h);
?>

programs.out:
$ php index.php
== read with fgets ==
  day 1: server up
  day 2: added route BRC
== read whole at once ==
day 1: server up
day 2: added route BRC
day 3: backup done
== w+ after truncate ==
  fresh start

expl.en: Same file, four moods: w rewrites from scratch (old content gone), a appends to the end, r reads with fgets + feof, and w+ truncates then lets you read back (rewind returns the pointer home). The file_get_contents/file_put_contents pair handles most cases in one call.

q.en: What two attributes does every form control need to submit data?

a.en: name (the key PHP sees) and value (what is sent); without name, the control submits nothing.

q.en: Radio vs checkbox?

a.en: Radios share one name and submit ONE value (gender); checkboxes are independent - use name="x[]" to collect many into an array.

q.en: Difference between text input and textarea?

a.en: Text input is single-line (name, city); textarea is multi-line with rows/cols (feedback).

q.en: Name three HTML5 input types and their benefit.

a.en: date / color / email / number - the browser shows a native picker and basic client-side checking.

q.en: What does the submit button actually do?

a.en: Fires an HTTP request to the form's action URL carrying every named control; no action attribute means post back to the same page.

q.en: GET vs POST - two key differences?

a.en: GET puts data in the URL (visible, bookmarkable, ~2KB limit); POST puts it in the request body (hidden, unlimited, required for uploads).

q.en: When should a form use GET?

a.en: For read-only actions: search, filter, paginate - anything you could safely bookmark.

q.en: Why must passwords never travel by GET?

a.en: URLs live in browser history and server logs - anyone with access reads the password.

q.en: What is $_POST?

a.en: The associative superglobal array of parameters sent in the request body of a POST.

q.en: $_REQUEST holds what exactly?

a.en: GET + POST (+ cookies) merged - convenient but vague; prefer the specific $_GET/$_POST.

q.en: Which superglobal tells you the request method?

a.en: $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] - 'GET' or 'POST'.

q.en: What does $_FILES contain per upload?

a.en: name, type, size, tmp_name, error - the facts PHP gathered about the uploaded file.

q.en: Why are superglobals 'super'?

a.en: They are visible in every scope - usable inside functions without global declarations.

q.en: Explain the self-processing page pattern.

a.en: One file: if REQUEST_METHOD==='POST' validate/process, else render the form; actionless form posts to itself.

q.en: What is a sticky form?

a.en: A form re-rendered with the user's previous values echoed back into each field (escaped) - fix one error, keep the rest.

q.en: Why validate on the server even with HTML required?

a.en: Client-side rules are hints that anyone can bypass; the server is the only trustworthy checkpoint.

q.en: isset() vs empty()?

a.en: isset checks the key exists (and isn't null); empty catches missing, '', 0, '0', null, false, [] - beware '0' counts as empty.

q.en: What does filter_var do with an email?

a.en: FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL returns the email if valid, false otherwise - one call replaces regexes.

q.en: Validation vs escaping - same thing?

a.en: No: validation guards INPUT (rules on arrival), escaping (htmlspecialchars) guards OUTPUT (safe echo). Both, always.

q.en: What does stripslashes() do?

a.en: Removes escape backslashes from text - mostly a legacy-magic-quotes cleanup, kept for completeness.

q.en: fopen modes r, w, a?

a.en: r: read (file must exist); w: write after truncating; a: append, creating the file if missing.

q.en: One-call alternatives to fopen/fwrite/fclose?

a.en: file_put_contents($f, $text, FILE_APPEND) to write, file_get_contents($f) to read, file($f) for an array of lines.

q.en: What does fputcsv do?

a.en: Writes one array as a proper CSV line - quotes and escapes commas/newlines correctly.

q.en: How do you list a directory's contents?

a.en: scandir($dir) (skip '.' and '..') or glob('uploads/*.png') for pattern-filtered lists.

q.en: mkdir gotcha?

a.en: Check is_dir() first and remember rmdir only removes EMPTY directories.

q.en: What does pathinfo() give you?

a.en: dirname, basename, filename and extension of a path - extension extraction without string surgery.

q.en: Which enctype does an upload form need?

a.en: multipart/form-data with method post - without it $_FILES stays empty.

q.en: Why must uploaded files be moved?

a.en: The upload waits in a temporary location (tmp_name) that PHP deletes when the request ends - move_uploaded_file() saves it permanently.

q.en: What checks before accepting an upload?

a.en: error === UPLOAD_ERR_OK, size limit, extension whitelist, getimagesize() to confirm image type, basename() the name.

q.en: What is basename()'s security role?

a.en: It strips directory paths from the submitted name (../../ tricks), so uploads cannot escape the target folder.

q.en: How does a page force a download?

a.en: Send Content-Type: application/octet-stream plus Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="x" headers, then the bytes (readfile).

q.en: mime_content_type or getimagesize - which for images?

a.en: getimagesize - it returns pixel dimensions too and proves the file really is an image.

q.en: mail() signature?

a.en: mail($to, $subject, $message, $headers) - headers carry From, Reply-To and the MIME Content-Type.

q.en: Plain vs HTML email?

a.en: Plain is the bare body; HTML adds the header Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 so clients render tags.

q.en: How are attachments sent?

a.en: MIME multipart: boundary, message part, then the file base64-encoded - in practice use PHPMailer.

q.en: Why does mail() often return false on XAMPP locally?

a.en: No SMTP server is configured for localhost - set sendmail.ini/SMTP settings (or Gmail SMTP) before it can send.
